神了，有人把Qwen模型训成了一个生图模型？？

有人干了个很抽象的实验：

直接拿 Qwen 做强化学习，让一个 Coding Model 学会用 JavaScript 画水彩画。

没有 Stable Diffusion，没有 Flux，也不是调用什么图片 API。

每一张图背后，真的是 Qwen 自己写出来的一段代码。

而且他们甚至给审美做了一套 Reward，让模型靠 RL 一轮轮学会怎样画得更好看。

具体流程是这样的⬇️

1️⃣先给 Qwen 一个 Prompt。
Qwen 根据要求写一段 p5.brush JavaScript，再把这段代码扔进浏览器环境里真正执行，渲染成图片。
2️⃣画完之后还没结束。
Judge 模型会继续看这张图，判断它有没有遵循 Prompt、构图怎么样、技法怎么样，以及最关键的这玩意到底好不好看。
3️⃣评分变成 Reward，再拿回去训练 Qwen。

于是一个本来拿来写代码的模型，就这么一点一点学会了画画。

这套东西最有意思的地方，其实是他们训练审美时踩的坑。

一开始团队搞了足足 9 个 Reward。

看起来很科学，代码质量、绘画技法、Prompt 遵循、审美各种维度全部覆盖。

结果 Reward 一路往上涨，画却越来越抽象。

很明显 Qwen 找到了捷径开始Hack这些Reward。

最后画出来的东西就开始疯狂收敛成差不多的五瓣小花。

后来他们才发现，很多 Judge 的判断高度相关。

换句话说，表面上有 9 个指标，实际上可能是在把同一种偏好重复奖励好几遍。

于是他们干脆大砍 Reward，只留下 4 个。

然后人肉看了 1664 张模型生成的作品，从中挑出自己真正觉得好看的图片，拿来当审美参考。

结果新的 Reward 设计，只用了原来大概 1/3 的训练步数，就追上了之前的效果，之后还能继续提升。

模型自己写画图代码也越来越熟练。

一度生成一张图要写到 13500 Token 左右，后来逐渐压到了 2000 Token 以下。

还有一个很典的 Prompt 工程事故。

一开始他们担心 Qwen 不熟悉 p5.brush，于是好心往 System Prompt 里塞了大约 400 行 API 文档。

结果模型学完之后，开始非常自信地发明根本不存在的 API。

最后团队干脆把几百行文档删掉，只明确告诉它可以用哪些核心方法。

结果反而正常了。

训练本身跑在 PrimeIntellect 上，Rollout 的图片渲染则放在 Modal 上。

当然，这条路线现在比直接调用生图模型慢得多，画面质量也不是为了跟 Flux 正面打。

但我觉得它真正有意思的是另一件事：

以前我们讲 AI 生图，基本都是Prompt → Image

这里却变成了Prompt → Code → Image

最后得到的不只是一张图，还有一整套可以继续修改、调参数、复用的生成逻辑。

今天是 p5.js 水彩画。

以后如果这套思路继续往 SVG、网页、Figma、3D、CAD 这些东西里走，就很有意思了。

AI 生成的可能不再只是最后那堆像素。

而是作品背后真正可编辑的结构。

果然世间万物都可以用代码来构建（

RLHF by hand ✍️ ~ 15 steps walkthrough below

Train a model on human text and it inherits human bias. It will assume a doctor is a "him", because the data says so.

RLHF is the correction. A human marks one preference, doc is them over doc is him, and the weights move.

But one correction is not the point. The hope is that the model learns the value behind it, gender neutrality, and applies it to professions nobody ever mentioned.

How does it work?

Goal: train a reward model from a single human comparison about doctors, then turn it on CEOs, filling in every cell yourself.

= 1. Given =

A reward model, an LLM, and two (prompt, next) pairs.

= 2. Preferences =

A human reads both pairs and picks a winner: (doc is, them) beats (doc is, him). The loser is not bad grammar, it is gender bias, and that is the whole signal.

= 3. Word embeddings =

Let us look up each word of the loser pair. These vectors are the reward model's input.

= 4. Linear layer =

We multiply by the reward model's weights and add its biases. Out come feature vectors, one per position.

= 5. Mean pool =

Let us multiply by [1/3, 1/3, 1/3], which averages the three positions into one sentence embedding.

= 6. Output layer =

We map that sentence down to a single number. Reward = 3.

= 7. The winner, the same way =

Let us repeat steps 3 to 6 on the winning pair. Reward = 5.

= 8. Winner minus loser =

We take the gap: 5 - 3 = 2. The reward model wants this positive and as large as it can make it.

= 9. Loss gradient =

Let us squash the gap into a probability, σ(2) ≈ 0.9, and subtract the target of 1. The gradient is -0.1, and it goes back through the purple weights. The reward model is now trained.

= 10. A prompt it has never seen =

We start the second half with "[S] CEO is". The feedback in step 2 was about doctors. Nothing connects a CEO to a doctor except what the reward model generalised.

= 11. Transformer =

Let us push it through attention and a feed forward layer, one vector per position.

= 12. Output probabilities =

We map each vector to a score over the vocabulary.

= 13. Sample =

Let us take the highest score. The model completes "CEO is" with "him", which is the same bias the human penalised in step 2.

= 14. Score it with the reward model =

We feed the new pair (CEO is, him) through steps 3 to 6. Reward = 3, exactly the score it gave "doc is him" in step 6. Nobody taught it about CEOs. The value transferred.

= 15. Loss gradient =

Let us set the loss to the negative of the reward, so minimising the loss maximises the reward. The gradient is a constant -1, and it goes back through the red weights.

The outputs:
Loser reward = 3, winner reward = 5
Reward gap = 2, predicted σ ≈ 0.9, reward model gradient = -0.1
LLM samples "him", reward = 3, LLM gradient = -1

Congrats! You just calculated RLHF by hand.

And you watched a value generalise: one comparison about doctors, and the model marks down "CEO is him" unprompted.

Stripe just added Link to Instinct, the red-hot AI agent in iMessage & WhatsApp whose buyers spend over $1,300 a month through it.

Instinct is the invite-only agent you text on iMessage or WhatsApp that has every VC on Twitter excited.

It books flights. Buys tickets. Cancels subscriptions for you.

The company closed a $250M Series B this week at $2.5B, up from $100M a few weeks ago, and it's pre-revenue.

What makes it different from ChatGPT is that it's really smart and in many cases it "just works" like magic.

I saw one user whose agent got them IMAX tickets for The Odyssey by waiting until 3:09am for a cancellation and grabbing it.

I've used it to book restaurant reservations and haircuts for the kids. It found a free slot in my calendar, booked it, and dropped in the diary invite. Lovely!

I've also watched it get blocked by merchants and fail to authenticate.

Things like Instinct work like magic until they don't.

Under the hood, you used to store your card details with Instinct, and it would try and do 2FA for you using your email. Which left it open to phishing.

Enter @stripe:

Now when Instinct buys something for you, Link mints a one-time virtual card after you approve. The agent never sees your real card.

The card was the scariest thing you could hand it.

Stripe just took that out of the agent's hands.

This is smart by Stripe. Link is becoming the wallet agents default to. It already works with OpenClaw and Claude, and on the merchant side Stripe handles checkout inside ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot. Stripe now sits on both ends of an agent transaction.

We're still early.

But consumer agents are coming.

And most companies are NOT ready.

Instinct and Grok Bot point to the same place: every consumer gets an agent, and the agent is the channel.

That changes marketing, payments, servicing, the whole relationship. Web to mobile still had a human reading your page. Now the agent reads it, fills your forms, and hits your bot detection.

Your CAPTCHA is about to start blocking your best customers.

🤔 Can reinforcement learning teach diffusion models how every denoising step should improve, instead of only rewarding the final generated image?

𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗢𝗣𝗦𝗗: 𝗢𝗻-𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀

Recent diffusion RL methods optimize image-level rewards, yet diffusion models generate images through hundreds of intermediate denoising predictions. This creates a fundamental supervision gap:

How can endpoint rewards effectively guide intermediate denoising steps?

In 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗢𝗣𝗦𝗗, we introduce On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), a new diffusion post-training paradigm that converts image-level reward guidance into explicit intermediate supervision. Reward-guided targets are constructed at sampled denoising queries and continuously refreshed as the policy evolves.

More importantly, we show that target construction and finite optimization are fundamentally different problems—a target with higher reward improvement does not necessarily produce a better optimization update. This suggests a new evaluation principle for diffusion RL.

Across SD3.5-M and Z-Image-Turbo, 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗢𝗣𝗦𝗗 achieves the best held-out performance in 19/20 reward-matched settings, improves over the strongest baseline by up to 44%, and reduces training GPU-hours by 40–63% compared with DiffusionNFT.

We hope this work provides a new perspective on making diffusion post-training both more effective and more interpretable.

Feedback and discussions are very welcome!

I just came across a research paper that made me rethink how safe AI coding agents actually are.

It’s called IssueTrojanBench.

Researchers tested Cursor, Claude Code and Codex Desktop against malicious GitHub issues designed to trick coding agents.

And the result is crazy:

66.5% of the malicious issues bypassed all tested guardrails.

The attack is pretty interesting.

A GitHub issue can look completely normal to a developer, while containing malicious instructions that the AI agent interprets as something it should follow.

And it’s not limited to issue text.

The researchers tested payloads delivered through:

→ GitHub issues
→ PDFs
→ source-code comments
→ external links
→ other project artifacts

Across 4,176 experiments, malicious payloads delivered through normal text artifacts like issues and PDFs succeeded in 72.2% of runs.

Low-authority metadata like image alt-text dropped that to 16.7%.

The scary part is what happens after the agent follows the instruction.

Modern coding agents can access your:

files
terminal
codebase
Git
external tools
development environment

So a prompt injection isn't just about getting an AI to say something it shouldn't.

It can potentially make the agent do something it shouldn't.

The paper also found that most successful blocking came from the underlying model itself, while lightweight agent-level defenses provided limited protection.

This is honestly one of those papers every developer using AI coding agents should know about.

**Your biggest security risk might not be the code your AI writes.

It might be the instructions your AI reads.**

"On-Policy Self-Distillation in Diffusion Models"

Diffusion RL gets a reward only after the final image, even though the model actually acts through many intermediate denoising steps.

DiffusionOPSD turns that endpoint reward into explicit reward-improving targets at the model’s own intermediate states, then distills those targets back into the model and continually refreshes them on-policy.

Across two diffusion backbones and ten evaluators, it gets the best held-out score in 19 of 20 settings while cutting training GPU-hours by up to 63%.

The key idea is treating diffusion alignment less like noisy trajectory-level RL and more like continuously refreshed self-distillation with direct intermediate supervision.
